title: Database Security
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 8: Software Development Security: Database Security.

items: Relational database — data organized in tables (relations) with rows (tuples/records) and columns (attributes/fields)
Primary key — unique identifier for each row in a table
Foreign key — field that references the primary key of another table; establishes relationships
SQL (Structured Query Language) — standard language for querying and manipulating relational databases
ACID properties of transactions:
Atomicity — transaction completes entirely or not at all (all-or-nothing)
Consistency — transaction brings database from one valid state to another
Isolation — concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other
Durability — once committed, transaction results survive system failures
NoSQL databases — non-relational databases (document, key-value, graph, column-family); designed for scalability and flexibility

blocks.text: Understanding database concepts is important for the CISSP because databases store the organization's most valuable data. Security professionals must understand both how databases work and how they can be attacked. Normalization is the process of organizing data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity. The normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF) progressively eliminate different types of data anomalies. While detailed knowledge of normalization levels is not required for the CISSP, understanding the concept of reducing redundancy to improve data integrity is important. Views provide a database security mechanism by controlling which data users can see. A view presents a virtual table that shows only specific columns or rows from the underlying tables. This supports the principle of least privilege — users see only the data they need.

items: SQL injection — the primary database attack vector; mitigated with parameterized queries
Excessive privileges — users with more database access than needed
Privilege abuse — legitimate users misusing their access
Database activity monitoring (DAM) — monitors and records database activity independent of the database engine
Encryption — encrypt sensitive data at rest (column-level or full-database encryption) and in transit (TLS)
Backup security — database backups contain all data and must be protected at the same level as the production database
Default accounts and configurations — disable default accounts, change default passwords, remove sample databases
Inference — deriving sensitive information from non-sensitive data through logical deduction
Example: knowing a department has 10 employees and 9 salaries, you can calculate the 10th
Defense: restrict access to combinations of data that could allow inference; careful query analysis
Aggregation — combining multiple pieces of non-sensitive data to derive sensitive information
Example: individually non-sensitive data points about military unit locations, sizes, and equipment combined to reveal classified troop strength
Defense: classification of aggregated data at a higher level than individual pieces; access controls on aggregate queries
Both attacks exploit the relationship between data elements rather than direct access to classified data

blocks.text: Inference and aggregation are particularly challenging security problems because they involve deriving sensitive information from data that is individually non-sensitive. Traditional access controls that protect individual data elements may not prevent these attacks. The key difference:

items: Inference: Using logic and reasoning to deduce information that is not directly available. The attacker uses known data plus logic to determine unknown data.
Aggregation: Combining many small pieces of individually non-sensitive data to build a complete picture that is sensitive. The whole is more sensitive than the parts.

blocks.text: Database security mechanisms to address these include: polyinstantiation, cell-level access controls, query analysis tools that detect potentially dangerous query patterns, and statistical database protections that add noise to query results. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Inference = deduction from existing data. Aggregation = combining non-sensitive pieces to create sensitive data. Both are database security concerns that traditional access controls don't fully address.

items: Polyinstantiation — allowing multiple rows in a database with the same primary key but at different security levels
Purpose: prevent inference attacks by providing different data to users at different classification levels
Without polyinstantiation: if a user with Secret clearance queries for a record and gets "no data found," they can infer that the record exists at a higher classification level (Top Secret)
With polyinstantiation: the user gets a plausible but different (possibly cover) record, preventing inference about the existence of higher-classified data
Adds complexity and storage overhead but addresses a real security gap
